label: Assumption audit
title: Assumptions and derived conclusions

checks.claim: The target is \(\Pi_N\propto e^{-V_N}\), with \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z^i)\).
checks.note: The reference probability measure is the normalized Gibbs measure for the displayed potential on the scaled particle state space. Its probability normalization is included in the LSI hypothesis.

checks.claim: The parameter noise is \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\), while physical particle noise is \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\).
checks.note: In scaled coordinates every noise coordinate has variance \(2\gamma/N\). Multiplication of each latent block by \(\sqrt N\) gives physical latent variance \(2\gamma\), while the parameter block is unchanged. Independence across particles, coordinates, and iterations identifies these updates with iteration of the Gaussian transition kernel.

checks.claim: The lifted dimension is \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and base smoothness \(L\) gives lifted smoothness \(NL\).
checks.note: The sum of the squared norms of the replicated parameter–latent pairs is \(N\) times the squared norm of the scaled state. Applying the pair-gradient Lipschitz inequality to this sum proves the gradient constant \(NL\). These calculations use no strong-convexity assumption.

checks.claim: The actual lifted target satisfies \(2\beta H\le J\) with \(\beta>0\).
checks.note: The LSI is assumed for the joint particle Gibbs measure with constant \(\beta>0\). An LSI for the distribution of one parameter–latent pair does not supply this hypothesis for a system whose particles share one parameter.

checks.claim: For \(D>0\), \(\beta\le NL\) follows from LSI and smoothness; \(0<\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) is the positive step restriction.
checks.note: In positive dimension, the ULA compatibility theorem applied with gradient constant \(NL\) gives \(\beta\le NL\). The step restriction is assumed explicitly. If the state dimension is zero, there is only one probability distribution, so the entropy bound follows from equality of the distributions.

checks.claim: At every positive interpolation time, the constructed density satisfies \(\rho_t=r_t\Pi_N\), where \(\rho_t\) is the law of the actual frozen-drift Gaussian step.
checks.note: Conditioning on the initial state gives a Gaussian centered at its deterministic gradient step. Integrating that Gaussian density over the initial distribution produces the positive interpolation density. Division by the positive Gibbs density gives its relative density.

checks.claim: The actual entropy is absolutely continuous on compact positive-time intervals and satisfies the proved entropy identity almost everywhere.
checks.note: The time derivative of the Gaussian kernel and the Fisher-information bound are integrable over every compact interval of positive times. Applying the weak equation to bounded approximations of the logarithm and passing the dominated limits gives an integral identity for entropy. Its integrable right-hand side proves local absolute continuity and identifies the derivative almost everywhere.

checks.claim: The actual Gaussian flux satisfies the spatial weak identity, and bounded entropy tests converge to the full entropy-production identity.
checks.note: Global integration by parts proves the weak equation for bounded continuously differentiable tests with finite gradient energy. The bounded logarithmic tests satisfy those conditions. Their limits are justified by the established energy bounds, rather than by assuming that the unbounded logarithm is an admissible test.

checks.claim: For the actual frozen update \(Y_t\), \(\mathbb E\|\nabla V_N(Y_t)-\nabla V_N(X)\|^2\le t^2(NL)^2G_k+2tD(NL)^2\).
checks.note: The centered Gaussian increment is independent of the initial state, so the mixed term in the squared displacement has expectation zero. Its second moment is \(2tD\). Multiplying the resulting displacement bound by \((NL)^2\) gives the displayed gradient-error estimate.

Write \(\ell=NL\). The Gibbs exponential moment of the squared gradient and the entropy variational inequality give an integrable squared gradient and \(G_k\le4\ell H_k+2D\ell\). Since \(\beta\le\ell\) in positive dimension and \(H_k\ge0\), enlarging the entropy coefficient gives the displayed estimate.

The initial relative entropy is finite by assumption. The shared one-step theorem proves that finite entropy at one iterate implies finite entropy at the next. Induction therefore gives finiteness at every iterate before any real-valued entropy bound is used.

Apply the ULA one-step entropy inequality with step \(\gamma/N\), dimension \(D\), gradient constant \(NL\), and LSI constant \(\beta\). The forcing is \(6(\gamma/N)^2D(NL)^2=6\gamma^2DL^2\), and the exponential factor is \(e^{-\beta\gamma/N}\).

Iterate the one-step recurrence and bound its geometric sum using the step restriction. Substitution of step \(\gamma/N\) and gradient constant \(NL\) gives the displayed coefficient \(8\). Finiteness of the output entropy is retained in the conclusion.
Divide the full-state estimate by the positive particle number \(N\). This divides both the initial-entropy term and the constant term by \(N\); the underlying joint relative entropy remains finite.

checks.claim: If \(\beta=N\alpha\), the normalized bias is \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\) and the rate is \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\).
checks.status: proved under the actual lifted LSI of strength \(N\alpha\)
checks.note: Assume that the joint particle target satisfies LSI with constant \(N\alpha\). Substituting \(\beta=N\alpha\) in the normalized bound gives the factor \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\) and the step restriction \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). The identity \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) gives the displayed dimension dependence.

checks.claim: Parameter KL is at most full joint KL; a bound \(H_k/N\le B\) gives parameter KL at most \(NB\).
checks.note: Apply data processing for relative entropy to the parameter projection of the joint distribution and target. The parameter divergence is finite and bounded by the full joint divergence. Consequently a bound on joint entropy divided by \(N\) must be multiplied by \(N\) before it bounds parameter entropy.

checks.claim: The proved conclusion concerns sampling error in relative entropy.
checks.note: The conclusion concerns relative entropy with respect to the Gibbs target. An estimate of distance from a marginal maximizer would also require concentration of the target and a comparison between that distance and entropy. Those results are not asserted in this extension.

verdict: The Gaussian IPLA entropy bound follows from differentiability of the pair potential, a Lipschitz gradient, an LSI for the normalized joint particle Gibbs measure, the stated positive step restriction, and finite initial joint relative entropy. Applying the ULA entropy theorem gives the density regularity, entropy derivative, initial-time bound, gradient moments, and discrete recurrence. The conditional theorems requiring interpolation data remain separate results. The proof assumes an LSI for the joint particle target; it does not derive that inequality from an LSI for a single parameter–latent pair. The conclusion bounds relative entropy and gives no concentration estimate about a marginal maximizer.
